newsitem.title: UK: Dlr buoyant in Europe amid Japanese, German woes.
newsitem.headline: Dlr buoyant in Europe amid Japanese, German woes.

text.p: The dollar remained buoyant against the mark and yen here Thursday as economic woes in Germany and Japan stayed at the forefront of traders' minds, suggesting no objection to recent currency trends from the Group of Seven industrial nations this weekend.

Persistent rumours that Japan's Nippon Credit Bank is in deep financial difficulty were denied by the bank later but proved enough to help dollar/yen to a fresh four-year high at 124.00 in early trade.
Dollar/mark, meantime, hovered just shy of 31-month highs as the mark was dented by yet another dire German jobless report.
Seasonally-adjusted German unemployment rose a massive 160,000 in January, dragging the unadjusted unemployment rate to 12.2 percent from 10.8 percent in December.

"There's really been no change in the fundamentals that have driven the dollar this far and it's highly unlikely anyone in the G7 has an interest to reverse the trend," said Peter Wood, currency trader at Bank of Boston.
"Quietly the Germans must be happy with a weaker mark when you see unemployment data like this."
At 1610 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6505 marks compared with 1.6490/95 late Wednesday.
Against the yen, the dollar was at 123.60/70 compared with 123.75/85 late yesterday.

The latest stream of official comments ahead of Saturday's G7 finance ministers meeting in Berlin again showed satisfaction with the recent rise of the dollar, even though traditional objections to volatility and the speed of its move were evident.

A German finance ministry statement released earlier said exchange rates would be discussed at the G7 meeting. It said recent moves were a normalisation and the talks would conclude that current conditions were favourable to continued growth.
A French official source concurred with this.

"We must consolidate this development (in world exchange rates) and reduce volatility," the French source told reporters. "We believe that the current situation is more in conformity with fundamentals."
As the dollar eased itself through an event-packed week, meantime, attention has turned to Friday's release of the U.S. January employment report.

Analysts polled by Reuters expect non-farm payrolls to rise 237,000 during the month after a 262,000 rise in December, providing a stark contrast in particular with the huge rise in unemployment seen in Germany.

The difficulty about the U.S. payrolls report for the dollar is that if it is much weaker than expected, pressure eases on the Fed to lift interest rates and this could undermine support for the unit. A much bigger-than-expected rise in jobs, on the other hand, risks irritating the stock and bond markets and denting the dollar indirectly on the day at least.
"The best number the dollar can hope for is one that is close to consensus because in the existing economic status quo the dollar will rise further," said a trader at a major Swiss bank.
Sterling and the Swiss franc were the other movers today, with the pound retreating and the franc bouncing.

The pound made an initial spurt higher against the yen, in particular, and also above 2.70 marks. It succumbed to a sharp bout of profit-taking later in the session, however, knocking it back below 2.70 and with sterling/Swiss franc sales eyed.
The Bank of England left key interest rates unchanged but this had been widely expected.

The Swiss franc made broad-based gains, meantime, and was helped by a report by independent Swiss economists who said the franc may be near undervalued levels. However, it also said any rise in the franc from here would be negative for the economy.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
